steps.text:
## Introduction

- Relay channel
  - three terminals: source (S), relay (R), destination (D); Fig. 1
  - source broadcasts to relay and destination; relay processes and forwards; destination joint decoding
  - classical protocols: amplify-and-forward (AF), decode-and-forward (DF), compress-and-forward (CF), + variations
  - AF: relay scales received signal and forwards; limitation: noise forwarding
  - DF: relay decodes to original bits, re-encodes; mitigates noise forwarding but limited when source-to-relay channel poor
  - CF: relay compresses received signal with Wyner-Ziv source coding, destination signal as side information
- Separation / JSCC
  - Shannon's separation theorem applies to relay channel (no side info at relay): separate compression + cooperative channel coding optimal with infinitely long blocks
  - holds even though relay channel capacity unknown
  - limited JSCC studies on relay channels: information theoretic study; JSCC for cooperative multimedia transmission, but with separate codes for compression and error correction, parameters optimized jointly for robustness to channel variations
- DNNs and DeepJSCC
  - DNNs applied to communication problems: channel coding, signal processing
  - DNN-based JSCC outperforms digital schemes with state-of-the-art compression + near-optimal channel codes; graceful degradation
  - DeepJSCC extended to text, video, point clouds
  - adapts to multipath fading, MIMO, multihop relay channels
  - no prior DeepJSCC work in cooperative relay setting; non-trivial extension; step toward JSCC in practical multiuser networks
- Our work
  - three schemes for image transmission over cooperative relay channel: DeepJSCC-AF, DF, PF
  - AF and DF resemble classical protocols; PF = variation of DF with simplified relay network, reduced complexity
  - AF: relay amplifies; destination uses maximum ratio combining (MRC)
  - DF: relay DNN reconstructs image, re-encodes into 'parity' symbols; destination concatenates with source 'systematic' symbols to decode
  - PF: like DF but no explicit reconstruction at relay -> less computation and delay
  - results: all beat digital baseline (BPG + polar codes), avoid cliff effect
  - DF/PF robust to poor source-to-relay channel; better than AF when source-to-relay channel strong

steps.text:
## Introduction

The relay channel has three terminals: the source (S), the relay (R), and the destination (D) (Fig. 1 shows an illustration). The source broadcasts its message to the relay and to the destination. Then the relay processes the signal it received and forwards it to the destination, and the destination does joint decoding to recover the original message. There are three classical relaying protocols, amplify-and-forward (AF), decode-and-forward (DF) and compress-and-forward (CF), and also variations of them. In AF, the relay just scales the signal it received and forwards it to the destination. The main limitation of AF is that it forwards the noise too. In DF, the relay decodes the received signal into the original bit sequence and then re-encodes it. DF mitigates the noise forwarding problem, but its performance is limited when the source-to-relay channel is poor. In CF, the relay forwards its received signal to the destination, but unlike AF it compresses the received signal first, using Wyner-Ziv source coding and treating the signal received at the destination as side information.

Shannon's separation theorem applies to the relay channel (when the relay has no side information). This means that separate compression followed by cooperative channel coding is optimal when the source and channel blocks are infinitely long. It is interesting that the separation theorem holds even though the capacity of the relay channel is not known. On the other hand, there are only limited studies on joint source-channel coding (JSCC) over relay channels. JSCC over cooperative relay networks has been studied from an information theoretic perspective. JSCC for cooperative transmission of multimedia sources has also been considered, but these papers use separate codes for compression and for error correction, and only their parameters are optimized jointly to get robustness against channel variations.

- DNNs and DeepJSCC
  - DNNs in communications: channel coding, signal processing
  - DNN-based JSCC beats digital (SOTA compression + near-optimal channel codes); graceful degradation
  - DeepJSCC extended to text, video, point clouds
  - adapts to multipath fading, MIMO, multihop relay channels
  - no prior DeepJSCC for cooperative relay; non-trivial; step to JSCC in multiuser networks
- Our work
  - DeepJSCC-AF, DF, PF for images over cooperative relay channel
  - AF: relay amplifies, destination MRC
  - DF: relay reconstructs image, sends 'parity' symbols; destination concatenates with 'systematic' symbols
  - PF: like DF, no explicit reconstruction -> less computation and delay at relay
  - all beat BPG + polar code baseline, no cliff effect
  - DF/PF robust to poor source-to-relay channel; better than AF when it is strong

## Introduction

The relay channel has three terminals: the source (S), the relay (R), and the destination (D) (Fig. 1 shows an illustration). The source broadcasts its message to the relay and to the destination. Then the relay processes the signal it received and forwards it to the destination, and the destination does joint decoding to recover the original message. There are three classical relaying protocols, amplify-and-forward (AF), decode-and-forward (DF) and compress-and-forward (CF), and also variations of them. In AF, the relay just scales the signal it received and forwards it to the destination. The main limitation of AF is that it forwards the noise too. In DF, the relay decodes the received signal into the original bit sequence and then re-encodes it. DF mitigates the noise forwarding problem, but its performance is limited when the source-to-relay channel is poor. In CF, the relay forwards its received signal to the destination, but unlike AF it compresses the received signal first, using Wyner-Ziv source coding and treating the signal received at the destination as side information.

Shannon's separation theorem applies to the relay channel (when the relay has no side information). This means that separate compression followed by cooperative channel coding is optimal when the source and channel blocks are infinitely long. It is interesting that the separation theorem holds even though the capacity of the relay channel is not known. On the other hand, there are only limited studies on joint source-channel coding (JSCC) over relay channels. JSCC over cooperative relay networks has been studied from an information theoretic perspective. JSCC for cooperative transmission of multimedia sources has also been considered, but these papers use separate codes for compression and for error correction, and only their parameters are optimized jointly to get robustness against channel variations.

Recently, deep neural networks (DNNs) have been applied successfully to many communication problems, for example channel coding and signal processing. Because DNNs are strong at extracting important features, they have also been applied successfully to JSCC problems. The resulting scheme was shown to outperform digital alternatives that use state-of-the-art compression techniques with near-optimal channel codes, and it also degrades gracefully as the channel quality gets worse. The DeepJSCC technique introduced in that work has been extended to other sources such as text, video and point clouds. Recent works also show that DeepJSCC can adapt to the more challenging multipath fading channel, the multi-input multi-output (MIMO) channel and the multihop relay channel. As far as we know, no prior work studies DeepJSCC in the cooperative relay setting. As we show in this paper, this is a non-trivial extension of the prior work, and it is an important step towards making JSCC real in practical multiuser networks.

In this paper, we propose three DeepJSCC schemes for image transmission over a cooperative relay channel, called DeepJSCC-AF, DF, and PF. DeepJSCC-AF and DeepJSCC-DF are similar to the classical AF and DF protocols in relay networks, and DeepJSCC-PF is a variation of DeepJSCC-DF that has a simpler neural network at the relay to reduce complexity. In DeepJSCC-AF, the relay amplifies the signal it received, and the destination node uses the maximum ratio combining (MRC) rule to combine the two received signals. In DeepJSCC-DF, the DNN at the relay reconstructs the original image and re-encodes it to make additional 'parity' symbols, which are forwarded to the destination. The destination concatenates the signals from the source (called 'systematic' symbols) with the ones from the relay to decode the image. DeepJSCC-PF is like DeepJSCC-DF, except that the relay does not need to explicitly reconstruct the image, so both the computation load and the delay at the relay are reduced. Our numerical results show that all the proposed schemes outperform the digital baseline, which uses BPG compression followed by polar-coded channel transmission, and they avoid the cliff effect. Finally, we show that DeepJSCC-DF/PF are robust when the source-to-relay channel is poor, and that they perform better than DeepJSCC-AF when the source-to-relay channel is strong.

## Introduction

The relay channel consists of three terminals: the source (S), the relay (R), and the destination (D) (see Fig. 1 for an illustration). The source broadcasts its message to the relay and the destination; the relay then processes its received signal and forwards it to the destination, while the destination performs joint decoding to recover the original message. There are three classical relaying protocols, amplify-and-forward (AF), decode-and-forward (DF) and compress-and-forward (CF) [1,2,3], as well as their variations [4,5]. In AF, the relay simply scales its received signal and forwards it to the destination; the main limitation of AF is the inherent noise forwarding. In DF, the relay decodes the received signal into the original bit sequence and then re-encodes it. While DF mitigates the noise forwarding problem, its performance becomes limited when the source-to-relay channel is poor. In CF, the relay forwards its received signal to the destination, but unlike in AF, it first compresses the received signal using Wyner-Ziv source coding, treating the signal received at the destination as side information.

Shannon's separation theorem applies to the relay channel (when there is no side information at the relay) [6]; that is, separate compression followed by cooperative channel coding is optimal in the limit of infinitely long source and channel blocks. Interestingly, the separation theorem holds even though the capacity of the relay channel is not known. On the other hand, there are limited studies on joint source-channel coding (JSCC) over relay channels. JSCC over cooperative relay networks is studied in [6] from an information theoretic perspective. JSCC for cooperative transmission of multimedia sources has been considered in [7]; however, these papers consider separate codes for compression and error correction, whose parameters are optimized jointly to provide robustness against channel variations.

Recently, deep neural networks (DNNs) have been successfully applied to a wide range of communication problems, e.g., channel coding [8] and signal processing [9]. Owing to their strong capability to extract important features, DNNs have also been successfully applied to JSCC problems, and the resulting scheme has been shown to outperform digital alternatives employing state-of-the-art compression techniques together with near-optimal channel codes, while providing graceful degradation with degrading channel quality [10]. The DeepJSCC technique introduced in [10] has been further extended to different sources such as text, video and point clouds [11,12,13]. Recent works show that DeepJSCC can also adapt to the more challenging multipath fading channel [14], multi-input multi-output (MIMO) channel [15] and multihop relay channel [16]. To the best of our knowledge, no prior work studies DeepJSCC in the cooperative relay setting, which, as we will show in this paper, is a non-trivial extension of prior work and an important step towards realizing JSCC in practical multiuser networks.

In this paper, we propose three DeepJSCC schemes, namely DeepJSCC-AF, DF, and PF, for image transmission over a cooperative relay channel. DeepJSCC-AF and DeepJSCC-DF resemble the classical AF and DF protocols in relay networks, while DeepJSCC-PF is a variation of DeepJSCC-DF with a simplified neural network at the relay for reduced complexity. Specifically, in DeepJSCC-AF, the relay amplifies its received signal and the destination node applies the maximum ratio combining (MRC) rule to combine the two received signals. In DeepJSCC-DF, the DNN at the relay reconstructs the original image and re-encodes it to generate additional 'parity' symbols that are forwarded to the destination, which concatenates the signals from the source (termed 'systematic' symbols) with those from the relay to decode the image. DeepJSCC-PF is similar to DeepJSCC-DF, except that the relay is not required to explicitly reconstruct the image, which reduces both the computation load and the delay at the relay. Our numerical results show that all the proposed schemes outperform the digital baseline of BPG compression followed by polar-coded channel transmission, while avoiding the cliff effect. Finally, we show the robustness of DeepJSCC-DF/PF against poor source-to-relay channel conditions and their superior performance over DeepJSCC-AF when the source-to-relay channel is strong.
